topic: Maurene Comey's firing ruled unlawful: can the attorney general fire a career prosecutor 'pursuant to Article II' and nothing more?
question: Did the Justice Department have the power to fire a career federal prosecutor without cause or process, as it argues, or did it break the civil service law and the separation of powers, as a federal judge ruled Monday?
summary:
On Monday, Oct. 26, Judge Jesse Furman of the Southern District of New York ruled that the Justice Department unlawfully fired Maurene Comey, a career assistant U.S. attorney who worked on the Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean Combs prosecutions and is the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey. She was fired in July 2025 by an emailed memo that cited only 'Article II of the United States Constitution and the laws of the United States.' In a 55-page decision, Furman held that the firing violated the Civil Service Reform Act, her Fifth Amendment due-process rights and the separation of powers. He ordered her reinstated retroactively, with back pay through Dec. 20, 2025, when she took another job.

The department did not claim misconduct or poor performance and admitted she had 'outstanding' ratings. Its argument was constitutional: the president's Article II power lets the attorney general remove prosecutors at will, and Congress cannot limit it. The department relied partly on the Supreme Court's June decision in Trump v. Slaughter. Furman wrote that this 'flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.' The department says it will appeal.

The ruling is not the last word. The Merit Systems Protection Board accepted a version of the same theory for fired immigration judges, and the full Federal Circuit is reviewing that case. Whether Comey was fired because of her father remains her allegation. The court has not yet ruled on that First Amendment claim.
verdict: Leans toward Comey's side on the checkable core. The department conceded the firing broke the civil-service rules, and the Supreme Court has never struck down a limit on removing an inferior officer. But the government's Article II theory is a live legal argument, not a frivolous one: one federal adjudicator has accepted it and an appeals court is weighing it. The claim that she was fired over her father is unproven. The meter cannot settle how much control a president should have over career prosecutors.
verificationNote: Furman's opinion itself was not read. CourtListener's docket returned a 403. Its holdings and quotes come from Fox News, CBS News and NBC News, which agree on the key wording, and from Government Executive. 28 U.S.C. § 542, United States v. Perkins and Myers v. United States were read at Cornell's Legal Information Institute. The Slaughter opinion was not read; its holding comes from law-firm summaries. The MSPB's immigration-judge ruling was confirmed in Government Executive and Justice Connection. Federal News Network and The Hill returned 403 errors, CNBC returned a 403, and NPR timed out. None of those were relied on.

left.label: A lawless firing of a career prosecutor
left.framing: A decorated prosecutor was fired with no reason, no notice and no hearing, apparently because of who her father is and after a social-media campaign against her. A judge has confirmed the law protects career prosecutors from that, and the president is not above the law.
left.strongestPoint: The government conceded the firing was not for cause and that the civil-service procedures were not followed, so the case turns entirely on whether Article II overrides a statute. On that question, Perkins and the Court's long practice of letting Congress protect inferior officers favor her.
left.weakestPoint: The motive story is presented as established. Her claim that she was fired because of her father or the Loomer campaign is an unadjudicated allegation. And many of the same voices praised a Democratic president's at-will firings in 2021 when the target was a Trump holdover.

right.label: The president runs the prosecutors
right.framing: Federal prosecutors wield the executive's most fearsome power, and the Constitution puts that power in the president. The attorney general has statutory authority to remove assistant U.S. attorneys, and the Supreme Court just confirmed that executive officers answer to the president. An Obama-appointed judge has put a career bureaucrat beyond elected control.
right.strongestPoint: The Article II argument is not invented. Prosecution is core executive power, Slaughter expanded presidential removal authority, and the full MSPB accepted a similar theory for immigration judges. The issue will be decided on appeal.
right.weakestPoint: It stretches Slaughter, a case about agency heads, to cover career staff, and it skips Perkins and the civil-service statute the department admits it ignored. Labeling the judge 'Obama' is a substitute for engaging his reasoning, and Republicans called a similar 2021 firing politicization when Biden did it.

facts.claim: The Justice Department did not fire Comey for misconduct or poor performance, and she had top performance ratings.
facts.evidence: CBS News: in court filings, DOJ 'admitted Comey received "outstanding" ratings from 2019 through 2024.' Fox News: the government conceded the removal wasn't based on misconduct or poor performance, and she got no advance notice or chance to respond.
facts.explanation: This is the government's own concession, so the factual core is not in dispute. The department's case rests on the claim that it needed no reason at all, not on any claim about her work. The department says then-Attorney General Pam Bondi directed the firing and her successor Todd Blanche ratified it.

facts.claim: Her termination notice gave no reason beyond Article II of the Constitution.
facts.evidence: NBC News (Sept. 2025): she was told by email she was terminated '[p]ursuant to Article II of the United States Constitution and the laws of the United States.' CBS News (Oct. 2026) quotes the same opening wording.
facts.explanation: Both sides rely on this. For Comey it shows no cause and no process. For the department it shows the firing was a constitutional act outside the civil-service scheme. In April, Furman used that framing against the department, holding that because it relied on Article II rather than the civil-service law, the case belonged in federal court, not before the MSPB.

facts.claim: Federal law gives the attorney general the power to remove assistant U.S. attorneys.
facts.evidence: 28 U.S.C. § 542(b): 'Each assistant United States attorney is subject to removal by the Attorney General.' Furman, quoted by NBC: 'Congress imposed limits on that power — limits that, even Defendants concede, were violated in Comey's case.'
facts.explanation: The statute grants the power, but the Civil Service Reform Act governs how it is used for career employees, requiring cause, notice and a chance to respond. The text alone does not make removal at will. The department did not rely on this statute to skip those steps; it relied on Article II.

facts.claim: Supreme Court precedent lets Congress restrict the removal of inferior officers appointed by department heads.
facts.evidence: United States v. Perkins (1886): when Congress vests appointment of inferior officers in department heads, 'it may limit and restrict the power of removal as it deems best for the public interest.' Furman, per Government Executive: the Court 'has never in its history found unconstitutional a congressionally imposed restriction on the removal of an inferior officer.'
facts.explanation: Assistant U.S. attorneys are appointed by the attorney general, which fits Perkins exactly. The government's best counter is Myers v. United States (1926), which struck down a Senate-consent requirement for removing a postmaster the president had appointed. Later decisions read Myers narrowly, and it involved presidential, not department-head, appointment.
facts.source: Cornell Legal Information Institute (United States v. Perkins)

facts.claim: The Supreme Court's June 2026 Slaughter decision allows at-will removal of career prosecutors.
facts.evidence: Consumer Finance Monitor: the 6-3 Roberts opinion held that 'officers exercising executive authority must remain subject to presidential supervision and removal.' CBS: DOJ 'relied partly' on that ruling; Furman called its position a 'sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority.'
facts.explanation: Slaughter overruled Humphrey's Executor for the FTC, a principal-officer case. Summaries read here do not show it addressing inferior officers or career staff. Government Executive reports critics saying the department treats dictum as precedent. Prosecutors do exercise executive power, so the extension is arguable. The Slaughter opinion itself was not read, hence medium confidence.

facts.claim: Another federal adjudicator has accepted the administration's Article II theory for fired Justice Department employees.
facts.evidence: Government Executive: in March 2026 the MSPB reversed an administrative judge and found inferior officers such as immigration judges may be removed at will if their duties stay within 'limited duties and no policymaking.' Justice Connection: the Board ruled 'the President's authority under Article II of the Constitution invalidates' the protections.
facts.explanation: The full Federal Circuit agreed on June 17 to hear the case, Jackler, en banc. Justice Connection, a group of former DOJ employees opposing the firings, concedes the loss, which strengthens the point. The MSPB is an executive-branch board, not a court, and the Federal Circuit may reverse it. Federal News Network's coverage returned a 403.

facts.claim: Comey was fired because she is James Comey's daughter, after a campaign by Laura Loomer.
facts.evidence: NBC News: the suit alleges she was fired because of her relationship to James Comey; Loomer posted that Comey and her husband should be 'FIRED from the DOJ immediately.' She was fired the day after being asked to lead a 'major public corruption case.' Fox News: Furman has not yet ruled on the First Amendment claim.
facts.explanation: The timing and the Loomer posts are documented, and the department has offered no other reason. But motive is exactly what the pending First Amendment claim will test, and no court has found it. Comey said she was told only that the decision 'came from Washington.' Monday's ruling does not depend on motive.

powerLens.thesis: The power test: would each side hold its view on removal protections if the other party's president were doing the firing? In July 2021 President Biden fired Social Security Commissioner Andrew Saul despite a statute allowing removal only for neglect of duty or malfeasance, relying on a fresh Justice Department legal opinion. The parties' arguments were the reverse of today's.

precedent.case: Biden's firing of Social Security Commissioner Andrew Saul, July 9, 2021
precedent.what: The Office of Legal Counsel concluded a day earlier that 'the President may remove the Commissioner of Social Security at will' and 'need not heed the Commissioner's statutory tenure protection,' reading Seila Law and Collins v. Yellen. Saul answered, 'I consider myself the term-protected Commissioner of Social Security.'
precedent.mirror: The mirror is imperfect: Saul was a Senate-confirmed agency head, the kind of officer Slaughter covers, while Comey was a career employee. That makes the 2021 firing an easier constitutional case than today's. The rhetoric still maps directly: a president setting aside a statutory protection on constitutional grounds, defended by his party and condemned by the other.

flips.then: Sen. Chuck Grassley on the Saul firing: 'There was no reasonable justification for these removals. President Biden is overtly politicizing the SSA.'
flips.now: The Republican administration fired a career prosecutor with no stated justification and argues in court that none is needed.

flips.then: Sen. Ron Wyden backed the Saul firing: 'Every president should choose the personnel that will best carry out their vision for the country.'
flips.now: Democrats now treat at-will removal under a constitutional theory as an abuse. Comey's lawyers call her firing a 'lawless, unconstitutional termination' and say 'the president is not above the law.'

powerLens.longRun: Strip out the parties and the durable question is where presidential control stops: at agency heads, at all officers, or at no one. Each party discovers the virtues of removal protection when the other holds the White House. After Slaughter, whichever party wins in 2028 inherits whatever line the courts draw for career staff, including the power to fire prosecutors investigating its own allies.
powerLens.appliedToScore: Neither side earns reasoning credit for its view of removal power as a principle, since both have argued the opposite when convenient. The needle rests on present-tense facts: the department's concessions, the statute, Perkins, and the unsettled status of the Article II theory on appeal.

pattern.thesis: Comey's case is one of many 'Article II' firings and one strand of the administration's actions toward people tied to its critics. Graded in isolation, it looks like one personnel dispute; seen together, the question is whether career employees have any enforceable protection from removals that cite only the Constitution.

campaigns.what: Two immigration judges fired under Article II lost before the full MSPB, which held inferior officers with limited duties removable at will. The Federal Circuit is hearing the case en banc.

Justice Connection counts more than 150 career employees fired on Article II alone; Government Executive reports 'hundreds' of DOJ workers subject to such firings. Both figures come from parties critical of the firings.

Her father's September 2025 indictment was dismissed in November because the prosecutor was found unlawfully appointed. A North Carolina grand jury indicted him again in April 2026 over the '86 47' seashell post.

pattern.takeaway: The recurring question is whether a president can turn the career civil service into at-will employment by citing Article II, and the Federal Circuit's en banc ruling will matter more than Comey's case. The one-off tell is anyone who discusses her firing only as a family story, or only as a lone activist judge, without mentioning the more than 150 similar Article II memos.

notAdjudicable: How much direct presidential control there should be over career prosecutors, which weighs democratic accountability against insulation from political pressure.
Whether a civil service protected from at-will firing is a safeguard of neutral government or an unaccountable bureaucracy, a judgment about institutions rather than fact.
Whether it is ever appropriate to remove an employee because of a relative's public conduct, which is a question of fairness that the First Amendment claim can address only in part.
Whether courts should order reinstatement of executive-branch employees at all, which turns on how one balances judicial remedies against executive autonomy.
biasWatch: The bias at work is judging the ruling by the name on it. To many on the left, 'Comey' makes the firing obviously retaliatory, so the motive claim gets treated as proven. To many on the right, 'Comey' and 'Obama judge' make the ruling obviously political, so the department's concession that it broke the civil-service rules goes unmentioned. The legal question would be identical for a prosecutor named Smith. The tell is any take that mentions her father or the judge's appointing president but never mentions the Civil Service Reform Act or Perkins.
